opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it really came out of a pretty practical frustration. We kept seeing that the models were getting smarter and smarter, but they were stuck in this little box. They only knew what was in their training data or what you pasted into the context window. And every time someone wanted to connect Claude to something real, like their codebase, their Google Drive, their Slack, or some internal database, they'd end up building a bespoke integration. Then the next team would build the same thing again, slightly differently, and none of it composed.

So you had this N-times-M problem: N models and M tools, and everybody wiring them together by hand. It reminded me of the pre-USB era, when every device had its own weird connector. The value of a standard isn't that any single integration is magic. It's that once you build a server for your tool, it works with any client that speaks the protocol, and vice versa. That's when you get a real ecosystem instead of a pile of one-offs.

A couple of folks on our team, David and Justin, had been prototyping this internally, and what convinced me was watching how quickly people started building on it once it existed. Engineers would spin up a server for some random internal tool in an afternoon, and suddenly Claude could use it. Intelligence is only part of the story. A really smart model with no access to context or the ability to take action is like a brilliant new hire who can't log into anything. MCP is how you give them the keys, in a structured way where you can still think about permissions and safety.

We also made a deliberate choice to open-source it rather than keep it as a proprietary Anthropic thing. If it's only ours, it's just another integration format. For it to be a standard, other model providers and tool builders have to feel like it belongs to them too. Seeing other companies adopt it was the moment I thought, okay, this is actually working.

r001.rationale: It describes teams repeatedly building bespoke integrations for models and frames a shared protocol as the way to avoid those one-offs.

r002.rationale: It says engineers could build a server for a tool and Claude could use it, but does not describe Claude writing integrations on demand.

r003.rationale: It mentions no initial skepticism, customer advisory board, or reaction to an MCP demo.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it came out of frustration more than vision. Inside Anthropic we kept watching the same thing happen over and over: a team would build a really nice integration between Claude and some tool, say a database or a ticketing system or Slack, and it would be bespoke. Every connection was a one-off. Then another team would need almost the same thing and they'd build it again, slightly differently. And customers were doing the exact same thing on their side. So the whole ecosystem was doing N-times-M work, every model times every tool, when the actual problem was pretty uniform.

The thing that made it click for me was realizing the hard part was never the model. The models had gotten good enough to use tools reliably. What was missing was the plumbing. If you think about how much value came from standards like USB or HTTP, it wasn't that they were technically brilliant, it's that they let people stop renegotiating the interface every time. I started seeing MCP the same way. You write a server once that exposes what your system can do, and any model that speaks the protocol can use it. That flips the economics for everyone building tools, because suddenly the integration is an asset instead of a cost they eat per vendor.

There was also a bet in there about where the value in AI was going to accumulate. A model sitting in a chat box with no context is actually pretty limited. Most of what people want is for the model to know about their stuff, their documents, their codebase, their calendar, and to be able to act on it. So the question of how models get connected to information wasn't a side feature, it was going to be the main thing. And if that layer was proprietary and fragmented, it would slow the whole field down. Making it open was partly principled and partly just practical. A standard nobody else adopts isn't a standard.

What surprised me was how fast it took off once it was out. I expected a slow grind of convincing people. Instead developers started building servers for things we'd never have gotten to, and other labs picked it up, which was the real test. When your competitors adopt your protocol, that's when you know it was actually solving a shared problem rather than just your own.

r001.rationale: The candidate says teams repeatedly built bespoke, one-off integrations and describes MCP as a common protocol to avoid that duplicated work.

r002.rationale: It says a server can be used by any model that speaks MCP, but does not describe Claude writing its own integrations on demand.

r003.rationale: The candidate mentions no initial skepticism from Ben Mann or an enthusiastic customer advisory board reaction to a demo.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is that a model is much more useful when it can connect to the context where you actually work. That might be your codebase, your documents, or a tool you use every day. But if every application has to build its own integration with every source of information, you end up duplicating a tremendous amount of work.

The value of MCP is giving those systems a common interface. A tool developer can expose a capability once, and different AI applications can use it. And the applications can support the protocol without having to anticipate every tool someone might want to connect.

That’s what makes a standard compelling to me: it lets people build independently and still have their work fit together. The model is one part of the system, but getting it the right context and giving it useful tools is a huge part of making it valuable.

r001.rationale: It says that building a separate integration for every application and information source duplicates work, and presents MCP as a common interface.

r002.rationale: It does not describe Claude writing its own integrations on demand using MCP.

r003.rationale: It does not mention Ben Mann’s skepticism or the customer advisory board’s reaction to an MCP demo.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the value comes from looking at what makes a model useful beyond the conversation itself. It needs access to the information you’re working with, and it needs tools that let it do something with that information. If every application has to build a separate integration for every data source and every tool, you end up duplicating a lot of work.

MCP gives those systems a common way to connect. You can build a connector once, and different applications can use it. That’s useful for developers, but it also opens up what users can do: the model can work with the context that matters to them, instead of being limited to whatever they paste into a chat.

The standard becomes especially valuable when people can build on it independently. You don’t need one company to anticipate every tool or every workflow.

r002.rationale: It says connectors can be built once and reused, but does not describe Claude writing integrations on demand.
